Common Grace (Doctrine)
KOM-un GRAYSS
noun (Reformed theology)
The Reformed-confessional doctrine of the non-saving grace of God shown to all creatures — the goodness by which God sustains the world, restrains sin, and bestows temporal blessings on the just and the unjust alike. Distinguished from special / saving grace. Developed substantially by the Dutch Reformed tradition (Kuyper, Bavinck).

📖 Biblical Definition

The Reformed-confessional doctrine of the non-saving grace of God shown to all creatures — the goodness, favor, and restraint by which God sustains the world, restrains sin, maintains order, and bestows temporal blessings on the just and the unjust alike, apart from the special saving grace given only to the elect. Common grace is distinguished from special (saving) grace: special grace is the saving, regenerating, justifying grace given only to the elect, by which they are brought to salvation; common grace is the non-saving grace given to all (the elect and the non-elect, the just and the unjust). The biblical foundation: (1) God's bestowal of temporal blessings on all — he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust (Matthew 5:45); he left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness (Acts 14:17); the LORD is good to all, and His tender mercies are over all His works (Psalm 145:9); (2) God's restraint of sin in the world — the restraining of human wickedness, so that fallen men do not sin as badly as they might (the restraint of God's Spirit, Genesis 6:3; the restraint of evil through the civil magistrate, Romans 13; the conscience and the work of the law written on the heart, Romans 2:14-15); (3) God's bestowal of natural gifts and abilities on all — the arts, sciences, government, culture, and the capacity for civic virtue and natural goodness among the unregenerate (the skill of craftsmen, the wisdom of rulers, the achievements of human culture). The doctrine of common grace was developed substantially by the Dutch Reformed tradition (Abraham Kuyper's three-volume De Gemeene Gratie; Herman Bavinck), explaining how the fallen world is sustained, how the unregenerate can produce relative goodness and cultural achievement, and how Christians can engage culture and cooperate with non-Christians in the common life of the world. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of common grace, distinguished from saving grace, against both the denial of common grace (which would deny any goodness or restraint in the unregenerate world) and the confusion of common grace with saving grace (which would treat the temporal blessings and natural goodness of common grace as salvific). Common grace explains the goodness, order, and cultural achievement of the fallen world, restrains sin, and provides the basis for Christian cultural engagement — while saving grace alone brings the elect to salvation.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Reformed-confessional doctrine of the non-saving grace of God shown to all creatures — sustaining the world, restraining sin, and bestowing temporal blessings on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17; Psalm 145:9); distinguished from special/saving grace; developed by the Dutch Reformed tradition (Kuyper, Bavinck).

COMMON GRACE (DOCTRINE), n. (Reformed theology) The non-saving grace of God shown to all creatures — sustaining the world, restraining sin, maintaining order, and bestowing temporal blessings on the just and the unjust alike, apart from the special saving grace given only to the elect. Distinguished from special (saving) grace. Foundation: temporal blessings on all (Matthew 5:45, his sun on the evil and the good; Acts 14:17; Psalm 145:9); restraint of sin (Genesis 6:3; Romans 13; the conscience, Romans 2:14-15); natural gifts and abilities on all (arts, sciences, government, civic virtue). Developed by the Dutch Reformed tradition (Kuyper's De Gemeene Gratie; Bavinck). Explains the goodness, order, and culture of the fallen world; the basis for Christian cultural engagement.

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 5:45 — "That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust."

Acts 14:17 — "Nevertheless he left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness."

Psalm 145:9 — "The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works."

Genesis 6:3 — "And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Common grace is the non-saving grace shown to all; the corruptions are the denial of common grace (denying any goodness or restraint in the unregenerate world) and the confusion of common grace with saving grace (treating temporal blessings and natural goodness as salvific).

expand to see more

The doctrine of common grace is held against two errors. The denial of common grace (associated historically with the hyper-Calvinist and certain strict positions, and the focus of the early-20th-century Dutch debate involving Herman Hoeksema and the Protestant Reformed Churches, who rejected the doctrine of common grace) would deny any genuine goodness, favor, or restraint of God toward the non-elect, holding that God shows no grace whatsoever to the reprobate; this struggles to account for the biblical witness to God's temporal goodness to all (Matthew 5:45; Psalm 145:9; Acts 14:17) and the genuine (if non-saving) goodness, order, and cultural achievement of the fallen world. The confusion of common grace with saving grace would treat the temporal blessings and natural goodness of common grace as salvific, or blur the distinction between the non-saving grace given to all and the saving grace given only to the elect; this obscures the particularity and efficacy of saving grace. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: common grace is the non-saving grace of God shown to all creatures (sustaining the world, restraining sin, bestowing temporal blessings, granting natural gifts and the capacity for civic virtue), distinguished from the special saving grace given only to the elect. Common grace explains how the fallen world is sustained and ordered, how the unregenerate can produce relative goodness and genuine cultural achievement, and provides the basis for Christian cultural engagement and cooperation with non-Christians in the common life of the world — while affirming that common grace does not save (only special saving grace brings the elect to salvation through the regenerating work of the Spirit and faith in Christ). The patriarchal-Reformed cultural vision (drawing on Kuyper) depends substantially on the doctrine of common grace: the world, though fallen, is sustained by God's common grace, and the Christian engages every sphere of culture under Christ's lordship, recognizing the genuine (if non-saving) goods that common grace produces.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The non-saving grace of God to all creatures (sustaining, restraining sin, temporal blessings); Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17; Psalm 145:9; distinguished from special/saving grace; Dutch Reformed development (Kuyper, Bavinck).
